prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff consumer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a debt collector's letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. A Collection Letter Violates the FDCPA If the Least Sophisticated Debtor Could Reasonably Read It to Have Two or More Meanings, One of Which Is Inaccurate.

Congress enacted the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to "eliminate abusive debt collection practices." 15 U.S.C. § 1692(e). Section 1692e bars "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt." *Id.* § 1692e. This Court has long held that whether a communication is deceptive is judged from the perspective of the "least sophisticated debtor." *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000). That standard protects "the gullible as well as the shrewd." *Id.* (citation omitted). It is "lower than simply examining whether particular language would deceive or mislead a reasonable debtor." *Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 454 (3d Cir. 2006) (citation omitted); *accord Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 221 (3d Cir. 2008).

Applying that standard, this Court holds that a collection letter is deceptive "where it can reasonably be read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455 (citation omitted); *accord Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221; *Tatis v. Allied Interstate, LLC*, 882 F.3d 422, 427 (3d Cir. 2018). Under this rule, a collector is not excused because the letter also has an accurate reading, or because a sophisticated reader would resolve the ambiguity in the collector's favor. The question is whether an inaccurate reading is reasonable for the least sophisticated debtor. If it is, the letter violates the statute.

### II. The Standard Is Objective and Does Not Depend on the Collector's Intent.

The inquiry is objective. The least sophisticated debtor is not a fool. This debtor is presumed to have "a quite modest level of sophistication," "a rudimentary knowledge about the financial world," and a "willingness to read a collection notice with some care." *Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 298–99 (3d Cir. 2008); *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221. Courts therefore reject "bizarre or idiosyncratic interpretations" of collection notices. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. But the standard exists to protect consumers who read carelessly or take statements at face value. *See Caprio v. Healthcare Revenue Recovery Grp., LLC*, 709 F.3d 142, 147–48 (3d Cir. 2013); *Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 997 (3d Cir. 2011). Because the test turns on how the letter could be read, a collector's good faith is no defense to a misleading communication. *See Allen ex rel. Martin v. LaSalle Bank, N.A.*, 629 F.3d 364, 368 (3d Cir. 2011).

### III. Defendant's Letter Satisfies the Two-Meaning Test.

The letter states [quote operative language]. [JA__.] One reasonable reading is that [accurate meaning]. But a second reading is equally natural to an unsophisticated consumer: that [inaccurate meaning]. That reading is inaccurate because [explain, with record support]. [JA__.]

This is not a "bizarre or idiosyncratic" interpretation. *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. It is the meaning that a debtor reading the letter "with some care" would most readily take from [the phrase/placement/formatting at issue]. *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221. Nothing elsewhere in the letter dispels the confusion. *Cf. Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455 (explaining that a letter's ambiguity is assessed by what the letter conveys to the debtor). The District Court erred by selecting the accurate reading and treating it as dispositive. *Brown* forbids that approach: once an inaccurate reading is reasonable, the inquiry is over, whatever other reading the collector intended.

### IV. The Inaccuracy Is Material.

A false or misleading statement violates § 1692e only if it is material, meaning it has the potential to affect "the least sophisticated debtor's ability to make intelligent decisions" about the debt. *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 421 (3d Cir. 2015) (citation omitted). The inaccurate reading here would lead a debtor to [pay prematurely / forgo a dispute / misjudge his rights or the amount owed]. [JA__.] That goes to the core of what § 1692e protects. This is not a "technical" misstatement that leaves the debtor's choices unaffected. *See id.* at 421–22.

### V. Conclusion

Because Defendant's letter can reasonably be read by the least sophisticated debtor to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate and material, it violates 15 U.S.C. § 1692e. This Court should reverse the judgment and remand for entry of judgment on liability for Plaintiff.
